Front: Port 20/21 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: FTP (File Transfer Protocol). Port 20: Data transfer. Port 21: Control/commands. Unencrypted - use SFTP (22) or FTPS (990) instead. Legacy protocol.

Front: Port 22 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: SSH (Secure Shell) - encrypted remote administration. Also used for SCP (Secure Copy) and SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol). Replaces Telnet for secure access.

Front: Port 23 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Telnet - unencrypted remote administration. Deprecated due to cleartext transmission. Never use in production - replaced by SSH (22).

Front: Port 25 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) - sending email between servers. Often blocked by ISPs for residential use due to spam. Use submission port 587 for clients.

Front: Port 53 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: DNS (Domain Name System) - translates domain names to IP addresses. UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers. Critical infrastructure protocol.

Front: Port 67/68 / Protocol: UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol). Port 67: Server. Port 68: Client. Automatically assigns IP addresses and network configuration.

Front: Port 69 / Protocol: UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) - simple, unauthenticated file transfer. No encryption or authentication. Used for: PXE boot, firmware updates, VoIP configs.

Front: Port 80 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) - unencrypted web traffic. Port 80 redirects to HTTPS (443). Should not transmit sensitive data over HTTP.

Front: Port 110 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: POP3 (Post Office Protocol v3) - retrieving email. Downloads messages to client, typically deletes from server. Unencrypted - use POP3S (995).

Front: Port 143 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) - accessing email on server. Keeps messages on server, synchronized across devices. Unencrypted - use IMAPS (993).

Front: Port 161/162 / Protocol: UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol). Port 161: Queries. Port 162: Traps (alerts). Manages network devices. Use SNMPv3 for encryption/authentication.

Front: Port 389 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) - directory services authentication. Unencrypted - use LDAPS (636) for secure authentication.

Front: Port 443 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: HTTPS (HTTP Secure) - encrypted web traffic using TLS/SSL. Standard for secure websites. Look for padlock icon in browser.

Front: Port 445 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: SMB (Server Message Block) - Windows file/printer sharing. Successor to NetBIOS. Used by: File shares, Active Directory, administrative shares.

Front: Port 587 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: SMTP Submission - clients sending email to server. Uses STARTTLS for encryption. Preferred over port 25 for client email submission.

Front: Port 636 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: LDAPS (LDAP Secure) - encrypted LDAP using SSL/TLS. Port for secure directory services authentication. Use instead of 389.

Front: Port 993 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: IMAPS (IMAP Secure) - encrypted IMAP. SSL/TLS encrypted email retrieval. Secure alternative to port 143.

Front: Port 995 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: POP3S (POP3 Secure) - encrypted POP3. SSL/TLS encrypted email retrieval. Secure alternative to port 110.

Front: Port 1433 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Microsoft SQL Server - database connections. Default port for MSSQL. Often targeted in attacks. Should be firewalled and not exposed to internet.

Front: Port 3389 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) - Windows remote desktop. Common attack target. Should use: VPN, NLA, strong passwords, account lockout.

Front: Port 5060/5061 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) - VoIP call setup. Port 5060: Unencrypted. Port 5061: Encrypted (SIPS). Manages voice/video sessions.

Front: Port 49 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access Control System Plus) - Cisco authentication protocol. Separates AAA functions. Preferred for device administration over RADIUS.

Front: Port 88 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: Kerberos - network authentication protocol. Uses tickets for SSO. Port 88 for KDC (Key Distribution Center). Default in Active Directory.

Front: Port 123 / Protocol: UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: NTP (Network Time Protocol) - time synchronization. Critical for: Logs, certificates, authentication. Should be secured (NTPS) to prevent amplification attacks.

Front: Port 135 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: MS-RPC (Microsoft Remote Procedure Call) - Windows communication. Used by DCOM, WMI. Often targeted in Windows attacks.

Front: Port 137-139 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: NetBIOS - legacy Windows networking. 137: Name service. 138: Datagram service. 139: Session service. Superseded by direct SMB (445).

Front: Port 162 / Protocol: UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: SNMP Traps - alerts sent from managed devices to SNMP manager. Asynchronous notifications of events (reboots, thresholds, errors).

Front: Port 179 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) - routing protocol for internet. Exchanges routing information between autonomous systems. Critical internet infrastructure.

Front: Port 201 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: AppleTalk - legacy Apple networking protocol. Rarely used today. May appear in legacy environments.

Front: Port 3268/3269 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Global Catalog (LDAP). 3268: Unencrypted. 3269: Encrypted (SSL). Used for Active Directory forest-wide searches.

Front: Port 500 / Protocol: UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: ISAKMP/IKE (Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol) - IPsec key exchange. Establishes VPN tunnels.

Front: Port 1701 / Protocol: UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) - VPN tunneling. Often combined with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec) for encryption. Port 1701 for L2TP alone.

Front: Port 1723 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: PPTP (Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol) - legacy VPN protocol. Considered insecure, deprecated. Do not use - replaced by IPsec, SSL VPNs.

Front: Port 1812/1813 / Protocol: UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service). 1812: Authentication. 1813: Accounting. Legacy ports: 1645/1646.

Front: Port 2049 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: NFS (Network File System) - Unix/Linux file sharing. Allows remote file access over network. Often used in Unix environments.

Front: Port 2082/2083 / What is the purpose?
Back: cPanel web hosting control panel. 2082: HTTP. 2083: HTTPS. Used for website administration.

Front: Port 2222 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Alternative SSH port. Sometimes used when 22 is blocked or for security through obscurity. Not true security - use proper hardening.

Front: Port 2375/2376 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Docker daemon ports. 2375: Unencrypted (insecure). 2376: Encrypted (TLS). Used for Docker remote management.

Front: Port 3000 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Common development server port. Used by: Node.js, React, Rails development servers. Should not be exposed in production.

Front: Port 3306 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: MySQL/MariaDB - popular open-source database. Default port for database connections. High-value attack target.

Front: Port 3389 / Protocol: TCP/UDP / What is the purpose?
Back: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) - Windows remote access. Common ransomware attack vector. Secure with: VPN, NLA, restricted access.

Front: Port 5432 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: PostgreSQL - open-source relational database. Default port for connections. Should be firewalled appropriately.

Front: Port 5900 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: VNC (Virtual Network Computing) - remote desktop. Cross-platform. Often less secure than RDP/SSH. Use tunneling or VPN.

Front: Port 5985/5986 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: WinRM (Windows Remote Management). 5985: HTTP. 5986: HTTPS. PowerShell remoting uses these ports.

Front: Port 6443 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Kubernetes API server - container orchestration. Secure port for cluster management. Critical for container security.

Front: Port 8080 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Alternative HTTP port. Common for: Proxy servers, application servers, development. Tomcat, Jenkins often use 8080.

Front: Port 8443 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Alternative HTTPS port. Common for: Web applications, Tomcat, alternative web servers. HTTPS equivalent of 8080.

Front: Port 9200/9300 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Elasticsearch. 9200: REST API (HTTP). 9300: Node communication. Search and analytics engine.

Front: Port 10000 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: Webmin - web-based Unix/Linux system administration. Alternative to command-line administration.

Front: Port 27017 / Protocol: TCP / What is the purpose?
Back: MongoDB - NoSQL database default port. Document-oriented database commonly used in modern applications.

Front: What is TCP vs UDP?
Back: TCP: Connection-oriented, reliable, ordered delivery, error checking, slower (HTTP, SSH). UDP: Connectionless, unreliable, faster, no ordering (DNS, VoIP, streaming).

Front: What is ICMP and its common uses?
Back: Internet Control Message Protocol - network layer for diagnostics. Uses: Ping (echo request/reply), traceroute, error messages (unreachable, time exceeded). Not for data transfer.

Front: What is ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)?
Back: Maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on local network. Required for Ethernet communication. ARP spoofing is common attack vector.

Front: What is DNSSEC?
Back: DNS Security Extensions - adds cryptographic authentication to DNS. Prevents DNS spoofing/cache poisoning. Signs DNS records with digital signatures.

Front: What is DHCP and how does it work?
Back: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol - automatically assigns IP configuration. DORA process: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. Reduces manual configuration.

Front: What is NAT (Network Address Translation)?
Back: Maps private IP addresses to public IP address. Types: Static (1:1), Dynamic (pool), PAT/Overload (many:1 with ports). Enables IPv4 conservation.

Front: What is PAT (Port Address Translation)?
Back: NAT variant mapping multiple private IPs to single public IP using different ports. Most common home router configuration. Also called NAT Overload.

Front: What is IPsec and its modes?
Back: IP security protocol suite for VPNs. Modes: Transport (end-to-end), Tunnel (gateway-to-gateway). Components: AH (authentication), ESP (encryption), IKE (key exchange).

Front: What is SSL/TLS?
Back: Transport Layer Security (successor to SSL) - encrypts network communications. Versions: TLS 1.2, 1.3 (current). Provides: Encryption, authentication, integrity.

Front: What is WireGuard?
Back: Modern VPN protocol. Simpler, faster than IPsec/OpenVPN. Uses state-of-the-art cryptography (Curve25519, ChaCha20, BLAKE2s). Growing adoption.

Front: What is HTTPS and how does it work?
Back: HTTP over TLS/SSL. Encrypts web traffic. Process: TCP handshake → TLS handshake (certificate exchange, key agreement) → Encrypted HTTP. Port 443.

Front: What is a VLAN (Virtual LAN)?
Back: Logical network segmentation at Layer 2. Creates separate broadcast domains on same physical infrastructure. Improves security and performance.

Front: What is a Subnet?
Back: Subdivision of IP network. Created with subnet mask. Enables network segmentation, reduces broadcast traffic, improves security and organization.

Front: What is CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)?
Back: IP addressing scheme replacing classful networking. Notation: /24 (255.255.255.0). Allows flexible address allocation. Example: 192.168.1.0/24.

Front: What is a VPN Concentrator?
Back: Device handling multiple VPN connections. Aggregates VPN tunnels, manages encryption/decryption, authentication. Used for remote access VPNs.

Front: What is AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting)?
Back: Framework for controlling access. Authentication: Verify identity. Authorization: Grant permissions. Accounting: Track activity. Protocols: RADIUS, TACACS+, Kerberos.

Front: What is CIA Triad?
Back: Confidentiality (prevent unauthorized disclosure), Integrity (prevent unauthorized modification), Availability (ensure timely access). Foundation of information security.

Front: What is DLP (Data Loss Prevention)?
Back: Technology preventing sensitive data exfiltration. Monitors, detects, blocks unauthorized data movement. Types: Network, Endpoint, Cloud.

Front: What is EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)?
Back: Security solution monitoring endpoints for threats. Features: Real-time monitoring, threat hunting, incident response, automated remediation.

Front: What is XDR (Extended Detection and Response)?
Back: Evolution of EDR collecting data across multiple sources (endpoint, network, cloud, email). Broader visibility, faster detection.

Front: What is IAM (Identity and Access Management)?
Back: Framework for managing digital identities and access. Includes: Authentication, authorization, user provisioning, privilege management, SSO.

Front: What is IDS (Intrusion Detection System)?
Back: Monitors network/systems for malicious activity. Types: NIDS (network), HIDS (host). Detective control - alerts but doesn't block.

Front: What is IPS (Intrusion Prevention System)?
Back: Monitors and can block malicious activity. Inline deployment. Preventive control - takes action against threats.

Front: What is MTTR (Mean Time to Repair)?
Back: Average time to repair failed component. Availability metric. Lower MTTR = better availability.

Front: What is RTO (Recovery Time Objective)?
Back: Maximum acceptable time to restore service after disruption. Business continuity metric. Drives DR planning.

Front: What is RPO (Recovery Point Objective)?
Back: Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. Determines backup frequency. RPO of 1 hour = backups every hour.

Front: What is NIST?
Back: National Institute of Standards and Technology - US agency developing standards. Cybersecurity frameworks: CSF, SP 800-53, SP 800-171 widely used.

Front: What is PII (Personally Identifiable Information)?
Back: Information identifying specific individual. Examples: Name, SSN, DOB, biometric data, email address. Protected by privacy regulations.

Front: What is PHI (Protected Health Information)?
Back: Health information protected by HIPAA. Includes: Medical records, health history, insurance info, billing data. Strict handling requirements.

Front: What is PKI (Public Key Infrastructure)?
Back: System managing public-key encryption. Components: CAs, certificates, CRL, OCSP. Enables: Encryption, digital signatures, authentication.

Front: What is SASE (Secure Access Service Edge)?
Back: Cloud-native architecture combining network security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA) with SD-WAN. Delivers security from cloud edge.

Front: What is SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)?
Back: Platform aggregating and analyzing security logs. Functions: Log collection, correlation, alerting, dashboards, compliance reporting.

Front: What is SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response)?
Back: Platform automating security operations. Orchestrates tools, automates workflows, enables automated response. Reduces analyst workload.

Front: What is SSO (Single Sign-On)?
Back: Authentication allowing access to multiple applications with one login. Improves user experience, reduces password fatigue. Protocols: SAML, OAuth, OIDC.

Front: What is ZTA (Zero Trust Architecture)?
Back: Security model assuming no trust by default. Principles: Verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach. Eliminates implicit trust.

Front: What is ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access)?
Back: Implementation of Zero Trust for network access. Replaces VPN. Grants access per-application based on identity and device posture.

Front: What is APT (Advanced Persistent Threat)?
Back: Sophisticated, long-term cyberattack by well-funded adversary. Characteristics: Stealthy, targeted, persistent, advanced techniques.

Front: What is AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)?
Back: Symmetric encryption standard. Key sizes: 128, 192, 256 bits. Replaced DES. Fast, secure, widely used.

Front: What is SHA-256?
Back: Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit. Cryptographic hash function. Produces 256-bit digest. Part of SHA-2 family. Secure for current use.

Front: What is MD5 and why is it deprecated?
Back: Message Digest 5 - cryptographic hash function. Considered broken due to collision vulnerabilities. Do not use for security - use SHA-256 or SHA-3.

Front: What is TLS 1.3?
Back: Latest Transport Layer Security version. Improvements: Faster handshake, removed weak algorithms, perfect forward secrecy mandatory, encrypted certificates.

Front: What is ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography)?
Back: Asymmetric encryption using elliptic curves. Smaller keys than RSA for equivalent security. Efficient for mobile/IoT devices.

Front: What is RSA?
Back: Asymmetric encryption algorithm. Based on factoring large primes. Used for: Encryption, digital signatures, key exchange. Key sizes: 2048-bit minimum.

Front: What is HSM (Hardware Security Module)?
Back: Dedicated hardware for secure cryptographic operations. Tamper-resistant. Used for: Key generation, secure storage, high-security environments.

Front: What is CRL (Certificate Revocation List)?
Back: List of revoked digital certificates published by CA. Clients check before trusting certificate. Can grow large - OCSP preferred.

Front: What is OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol)?
Back: Protocol for real-time certificate status checking. Faster than CRL. Client queries responder to check if certificate is valid.

Front: What is CSR (Certificate Signing Request)?
Back: Message sent to CA to request digital certificate. Contains public key and identifying information. CA signs and returns certificate.

Front: What is CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker)?
Back: Security policy enforcement point between cloud users and providers. Functions: Visibility, compliance, threat protection, data security.

Front: What is SWG (Secure Web Gateway)?
Back: Security solution filtering web traffic. Protects against: Malware, phishing, data loss. Features: URL filtering, SSL inspection, DLP.

Front: What is WAF (Web Application Firewall)?
Back: Firewall protecting web applications. Inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic. Blocks: SQLi, XSS, CSRF. Network, host, or cloud-based.

Front: What is NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall)?
Back: Advanced firewall with deep inspection, application awareness, IPS, threat intelligence. Beyond traditional port/protocol filtering.

Front: What is UTM (Unified Threat Management)?
Back: All-in-one security appliance. Combines: Firewall, IDS/IPS, VPN, antivirus, content filtering. Simpler but may lack depth of specialized tools.

Front: What is NAC (Network Access Control)?
Back: Controls device network access based on posture. Verifies: Antivirus, patches, configuration. Can quarantine non-compliant devices.

Front: What is PAM (Privileged Access Management)?
Back: Manages elevated access accounts. Features: Password vaulting, session recording, just-in-time access. Protects admin/root accounts.

Front: What is RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)?
Back: Access control based on user roles. Permissions assigned to roles, users assigned to roles. Simplifies administration in large organizations.

Front: What is ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control)?
Back: Access control based on attributes of user, resource, environment. Dynamic policies using multiple factors. More flexible than RBAC.

Front: What is MAC (Mandatory Access Control)?
Back: Access control enforced by system based on security labels. Users cannot override. Used in: Military, high-security environments.

Front: What is DAC (Discretionary Access Control)?
Back: Access control where resource owner decides permissions. Common in consumer systems. Flexible but less secure than MAC.

Front: What is SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)?
Back: XML-based protocol for SSO. Identity Provider authenticates, sends assertion to Service Provider. Common in enterprise.

Front: What is OAuth 2.0?
Back: Authorization framework for delegated access. User grants application access without sharing password. Not authentication protocol.

Front: What is OIDC (OpenID Connect)?
Back: Authentication layer on OAuth 2.0. Provides identity verification using ID tokens (JWT). Combines authn and authz.

Front: What is LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)?
Back: Protocol for accessing directory services. Stores: Users, groups, attributes. Common implementations: Active Directory, OpenLDAP.

Front: What is Kerberos?
Back: Network authentication using tickets. Provides SSO. Components: KDC, TGT, service tickets. Default in Active Directory.

Front: What is RADIUS?
Back: Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service. Centralized authentication for network access. Uses UDP. Common for VPN, wireless.

Front: What is TACACS+?
Back: Cisco authentication protocol. Separates AAA functions. Uses TCP. Preferred for device administration.

Front: What is MFA (Multifactor Authentication)?
Back: Requiring multiple authentication factors. Factors: Knowledge, possession, inherence, location, behavior. Stronger than single factor.

Front: What is FIDO2?
Back: Standard for passwordless authentication. Uses: Security keys, biometrics, platform authenticators. Phishing-resistant.

Front: What is CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System)?
Back: Standard for rating vulnerability severity. Scores 0-10. Factors: Exploitability, impact, scope. Helps prioritize patching.

Front: What is CVE (Common Vulnerability Enumeration)?
Back: Standard identifier for vulnerabilities. Format: CVE-YEAR-NUMBER. Enables consistent reference across tools.

Front: What is OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence)?
Back: Intelligence from publicly available sources. Used in: Reconnaissance, threat intelligence, investigations. Legal and ethical.

Front: What is IoC (Indicator of Compromise)?
Back: Evidence of potential security incident. Examples: IP addresses, file hashes, domains, registry keys. Used for detection and hunting.

Front: What is TTP (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures)?
Back: Behavior patterns of threat actors. Tactics: Adversary goals. Techniques: Methods. Procedures: Specific implementations. MITRE ATT&CK framework organizes TTPs.

Front: What is BCP (Business Continuity Plan)?
Back: Plan maintaining critical business functions during disruption. Broader than IT - includes facilities, personnel, suppliers.

Front: What is DRP (Disaster Recovery Plan)?
Back: IT-focused plan for recovering technology after disaster. Subset of BCP. Covers: Backups, recovery, alternate sites.

Front: What is IRP (Incident Response Plan)?
Back: Plan for responding to security incidents. Defines: Roles, procedures, communication, escalation. Should be tested regularly.

Front: What is BIA (Business Impact Analysis)?
Back: Process identifying critical functions and dependencies. Determines: RTO, RPO, resource needs. Foundation for BCP/DRP.

Front: What is GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)?
Back: EU regulation protecting personal data. Requirements: Consent, data minimization, right to erasure, breach notification. Heavy fines.

Front: What is HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)?
Back: US law protecting health information. Applies to healthcare providers, insurers, business associates. Administrative, physical, technical safeguards.

Front: What is PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)?
Back: Standard for credit card handlers. 12 requirements. Non-compliance = fines, loss of processing ability.

Front: What is SOC 2 (Service Organization Control 2)?
Back: Audit report on service organization controls. Trust Services Criteria: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy.

Front: What is ISO 27001?
Back: International standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS). Requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining security. Certifiable.

Front: What is CIS Controls?
Back: Center for Internet Security's 18 prioritized security controls. Practical, actionable guidance organized by Implementation Groups.

Front: What is CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification)?
Back: US DoD program for defense contractors. Five maturity levels. Third-party assessment required for CUI contracts.

Front: What is SLA (Service Level Agreement)?
Back: Contract defining service expectations. Includes: Availability, response times, penalties. Security SLAs may include patch timelines.

Front: What is NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement)?
Back: Contract protecting confidential information. Prevents disclosure during and after relationship. Critical for vendors, employees.

Front: What is MOU (Memorandum of Understanding)?
Back: Non-binding agreement outlining intentions. Less formal than contract. Often used between government entities.

Front: What is MSA (Master Service Agreement)?
Back: Overarching contract defining ongoing relationship terms. Individual Work Orders for specific services.

Front: What is AUP (Acceptable Use Policy)?
Back: Policy defining acceptable IT resource use. Users typically sign before access. Covers: Internet, email, devices, software.

Front: What is BYOD (Bring Your Own Device)?
Back: Policy allowing personal devices for work. Benefits: Cost savings, user satisfaction. Risks: Security, compliance, privacy.

Front: What is COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled)?
Back: Company provides device, personal use allowed. Balance of control and flexibility. Common enterprise approach.

Front: What is CYOD (Choose Your Own Device)?
Back: User selects from approved device list. Company owns device. Balance of choice and standardization.

Front: What is MDM (Mobile Device Management)?
Back: Software managing mobile devices. Capabilities: Remote wipe, policy enforcement, app management, encryption.

Front: What is UEM (Unified Endpoint Management)?
Back: Managing all endpoints (mobile, desktop, IoT) from single platform. Evolution of MDM/MAM.

Front: What is SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol)?
Back: Standards for automated vulnerability management. Components: CVE, CVSS, CCE, CPE, XCCDF, OVAL.

Front: What is STIX/TAXII?
Back: STIX: Structured Threat Information eXpression - threat intel format. TAXII: Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information - sharing protocol.

Front: What is ATT&CK (MITRE ATT&CK)?
Back: Knowledge base of adversary TTPs. Organized by tactics (goals) and techniques (methods). Used for: Threat modeling, detection, hunting.

Front: What is SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response)?
Back: Platform automating security operations. Orchestrates tools, automates workflows, enables automated response.

Front: What is UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics)?
Back: Monitoring user and device behavior to detect anomalies. ML-based baselining. Detects: Compromised accounts, insider threats.

Front: What is FIM (File Integrity Monitoring)?
Back: Tracking changes to critical files. Alerts on unauthorized modifications. Compliance requirement, detects malware.

Front: What is DLP (Data Loss Prevention)?
Back: Preventing sensitive data exfiltration. Types: Network, Endpoint, Cloud. Uses content inspection, pattern matching.

Front: What is IaaS/PaaS/SaaS?
Back: Cloud service models. IaaS: Infrastructure (most control). PaaS: Platform (middle). SaaS: Software (least control). Shared responsibility varies.

Front: What is IaC (Infrastructure as Code)?
Back: Managing infrastructure through code files. Benefits: Version control, consistency, automation. Tools: Terraform, CloudFormation.

Front: What is SDN (Software-Defined Networking)?
Back: Separating control plane from data plane. Centralized, programmable network management.

Front: What is SD-WAN?
Back: Software-Defined Wide Area Network. Centralized WAN management. Benefits: Cost reduction, improved performance, security.

Front: What is SASE (Secure Access Service Edge)?
Back: Cloud-native security architecture. Combines: SWG, CASB, ZTNA, SD-WAN. Delivers security from cloud edge.

Front: What is ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access)?
Back: Zero Trust implementation for network access. Replaces VPN. Per-application access based on identity and posture.

Front: What is EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)?
Back: Endpoint security solution. Features: Real-time monitoring, threat hunting, incident response, automated remediation.

Front: What is XDR (Extended Detection and Response)?
Back: EDR extended across multiple sources. Broader visibility, faster detection. Correlates endpoint, network, cloud, email.

Front: What is MDR (Managed Detection and Response)?
Back: Outsourced security service. Provider monitors and responds to threats on customer's behalf. 24/7 coverage.

Front: What is MSSP (Managed Security Service Provider)?
Back: Outsourced security monitoring and management. Services: SOC, SIEM, vulnerability management, compliance.

Front: What is MSP (Managed Service Provider)?
Back: Outsourced IT management. May include security. Broader than MSSP - includes general IT services.

Front: What is CSP (Cloud Service Provider)?
Back: Company providing cloud services. Examples: AWS, Azure, GCP. Shared responsibility model applies.

Front: What is MSS (Managed Security Services)?
Back: Outsourced security operations. Includes: Monitoring, management, response. Provides expertise without building internal team.

Front: What is CIRT/CSIRT (Computer Incident Response Team)?
Back: Team responsible for incident response. Handles: Detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.

Front: What is SOC (Security Operations Center)?
Back: Centralized team monitoring and responding to security events. 24/7 operations. Uses: SIEM, threat intel, playbooks.

Front: What is NOC (Network Operations Center)?
Back: Team monitoring network infrastructure. Focuses on availability and performance. May work with SOC on security events.

Front: What is CISO (Chief Information Security Officer)?
Back: Executive responsible for security strategy and program. Reports to board, manages security team, ensures compliance.

Front: What is CIO (Chief Information Officer)?
Back: Executive responsible for IT strategy and operations. May oversee security or work alongside CISO.

Front: What is CTO (Chief Technology Officer)?
Back: Executive responsible for technology strategy and development. Focuses on product/technical innovation.

Front: What is DPO (Data Protection Officer)?
Back: Role required by GDPR. Oversees data protection strategy, ensures compliance, point of contact for regulators.

Front: What is ISSO (Information Systems Security Officer)?
Back: Role managing security for specific system or program. Implements security controls, ensures compliance.
